line: I walk out to the flat stone mid-ford and wait there with my hands empty and the pendant bright at my throat, the psalter tucked under my arm in plain sight. When the wagon stops on the bank, I call across the water, calm and clear enough for Hob and the villagers to hear. "Master Tallowmere, you wrote to me, so you can come to me. Bring your own two feet and leave Garrow on the bank."

entries.text: dice Wren's Persuasion/Performance-style command carrying across the ford, to make Corvin come alone, DC 13: 1d20+5 = 1d20 [3] + 5 = 8

input.add_to_description: Day 5 ~5:30 PM at the ford: Corvin climbed down from the wagon, tall, silver-haired, clove-scented, with a kind smile. He answered Wren's call by walking out alone onto the stones, but sent Garrow along the bank "to keep the water-side clear" rather than leaving him, and the driver stays on the box with a crossbow under the seat. He keeps his hands open and speaks gently.

entries.text:
You stand on the flat stone with the water sliding past your boots and the psalter under your arm, and you call it out across the ford, clear and level. Your Persuasion check was an 8, and it only half carries.

The wagon stops on the bank. A tall man climbs down from the box, silver-haired, in a long dark coat, with the faint scent of clove drifting on the evening air. Corvin. He looks older than you remember, and kinder, which is the worst part. He raises both open hands to the villagers on the bank as if greeting a congregation, then to you.

"My girl," he says, and the voice is the one that sang you to sleep for nineteen years. "Of course. My own two feet." He steps onto the first stone, then the second, light and unhurried. But he does not send Garrow back. The brown-coated man drifts along the near bank with an easy smile, "keeping the water-side clear," as Corvin calls over his shoulder, and the driver stays on the wagon box with one hand tucked beneath the seat where you remember a crossbow being kept.

Hob sits by his green door with his pipe unlit. Villagers hover on the bank. In the willows, Alder and Kit haven't moved. Corvin reaches the stone beside yours, close enough to touch, and stops. His eyes drop to the silver lantern at your throat, and for a moment something crosses his face, quick as a fish under ice.

"Well," he says softly. "She gave it to you after all."

The sun is touching the spur. You have the ledger, Elowen's letter, her commission, and a crowd to hear it. What does Wren say?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

line: I walk out to the flat stone mid-ford and wait there with my hands empty and the pendant bright at my throat, the psalter tucked under my arm in plain sight. When the wagon stops on the bank, I call across the water, calm and clear enough for Hob and the villagers to hear. "Master Tallowmere, you wrote to me, so you can come to me. entries.text: dice Wren's Intimidation-free Persuasion/Performance command across the water, calm and clear (Performance), DC 12: 1d20+5 = 1d20 [12] + 5 = 17

Your Performance check was a 17. Your voice carries over the water as clear as a bell, and every head on the bank turns. Hob takes his pipe from his mouth. Along the shore, the villagers go quiet.

The wagon creaks to a halt on the far bank. The driver sits rigid on the box. Garrow stops where he stands, glancing back at the wagon's canvas, and doesn't move again.

The canvas parts. Corvin Tallowmere steps down, and he's exactly as you left him. He's a tall man in a fine, plain coat, silver-streaked at the temples, with warm dark eyes and a voice made for firelit rooms. He carries no weapon, only a small iron key on a cord at his neck, and he looks at you across the shining water with something that might be pride.

"Wren," he calls, not loudly, because he doesn't need to. "Well said. Leave Garrow, she says. Very well." He lifts a hand, and Garrow takes a step back, his smile gone thin. Then Corvin takes off his boots, ties them together, and wades out onto the stepping stones, barefoot, unhurried, the water curling about his ankles.

"You've been busy, my girl," he says, coming on. "A confession at the Heron and Net. A coffer opened in a strongroom." He stops three stones off and looks at the pendant at your throat. The smile falters, just slightly. "So she kept her promise to you after all. Elowen. I wondered if she would."

The light is turning gold on the water. Hob is listening. Alder and Kit are somewhere in the willows. Corvin waits a stone's length away, with the key at his neck and the whole river behind him.

What does Wren say or do?

input.add_to_description: Day 5 ~5:30 PM: met Wren mid-ford after her call (23). Silver-haired, sixtyish, clove-and-ink scent, gentle voice. Sent Garrow back and the driver kept the wagon on the bank. Walks out alone across the stones. Has not yet spoken.

entries.text:
Your voice carries over the water like a bell, and your check was a 23. On the bank the wagon stops. The driver sits stiff on the box. Garrow, a pace ahead, stops mid-stride and looks to the wagon's shadow.

A curtain moves. Corvin Tallowmere climbs down.

He is older than you remember, silver-haired and neat in a travelling coat, with a staff he doesn't lean on. He lifts one hand, and Garrow stops as if on a string. Then he walks out onto the stepping stones alone, unhurried, the water flashing around his boots, a man crossing a stage he built himself. On the bank, villagers murmur. Hob Crannock's pipe has gone out. In the willows, nothing moves.

He stops two stones short of you, and the smell reaches you first, clove and ink. His eyes go to your throat, to the pendant, and something in his face closes and opens again.

"You've been busy, my girl," he says gently. "You've opened her coffer. Then you know I didn't lie about the parchment." He glances at the psalter under your arm. "I did come to talk like family. But I think you'd better tell me first what you mean to do with what you know."

The ford murmurs. Dusk is still a half hour off, and every eye on the bank is on the two of you. What does Wren say?

input.add_to_description: Day 5 ~5:20 PM: appears at the ford, a tall silver-haired man in a travelling coat, warm voice, clove-and-ink scent. Wren's Persuasion 13 (one short of 14): he comes onto the stones alone and unarmed-looking, but leaves Garrow within a bowshot on the bank, hand on a hidden crossbow, and the driver at the wagon. He greets her as "my girl" and says Elowen's name first.

entries.text:
The wagon halts on the bank with a groan of axles. Your call carries over the water, clear enough that Hob takes his pipe from his mouth and the villagers by the willows go still. Your Persuasion check was a 13, one short of what it needed.

Corvin steps down. He's tall and silver-haired in a good travelling coat, with the same warm, unhurried smile, and the clove-and-ink scent reaches you before he does. He walks out along the stepping stones with his hands visible and nothing in them, easy as a man crossing his own parlour. Garrow doesn't stay where you told him. He hangs back on the bank, but only to a bowshot, and there's a bulge under his brown coat that you'd bet is a crossbow. The driver stays with the wagon.

Corvin stops a stone away. The water chuckles between you.

"Elowen's girl," he says softly. "You've her way of standing, you know. Feet apart, as though the world might tip." His eyes drop to the pendant and stay there. "So the lamp finally opened the box. I wondered if it ever would." Then his gaze comes back up, and the smile is gone. "I did not kill her, Wren. Whatever she wrote. I'd like you to hear that first, before the villagers decide what to do with me."

He nods at the psalter under your arm. "That's what I came for, but I think we both know it isn't what you came for. Ask me what you really want to ask."

Behind him, the sun touches the spur. What does Wren say or do?
